question_text: Why can small model errors scale quickly in finance, according to the lecture?
hint: Think about what financial systems are connected to.
correct_answer_citation: Week 03 — Why Finance Became an AI Domain

options.option_text: Financial data is too sparse for models to learn any stable patterns.
options.option_explanation: The lecture says the opposite: digital channels, machine-readable records, and high-frequency workflows create dense operational signals.

options.option_text: Each financial decision is made only once, so errors are never repeated.
options.option_explanation: Finance runs on repeated decisions under uncertainty: approve, price, monitor, flag, hedge, and allocate.

options.option_text: Financial systems are linked to capital, compliance, and customer trust.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Small model errors can scale quickly because financial systems are linked to capital, compliance, and customer trust.

options.option_text: Digital channels have removed most of the human review from financial firms.
options.option_explanation: The lecture does not say human review has been removed. It ties the scaling of errors to the links between financial systems and capital, compliance, and customer trust.

question_text: What role does the lecture give generative models in financial tasks?
hint: The lecture lists what they support, then names what they should not become.
correct_answer_citation: Week 03 — Matching Method to Financial Task

options.option_text: They support summarization, drafting, and copilots, not final authority.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Generative models support summarization, drafting, extraction, scenario narration, and analyst copilots rather than final authority.

options.option_text: They replace supervised learning for default prediction and fraud scoring.
options.option_explanation: Default prediction and fraud scoring are listed under supervised learning, not generative models.

options.option_text: They surface anomalies and clusters in network data when labels are weak.
options.option_explanation: That describes unsupervised methods, which help surface anomalies, clusters, and unusual network behavior when labels are weak.

options.option_text: They act as the final authority once a scenario narration has been drafted.
options.option_explanation: The lecture says generative models support scenario narration and analyst copilots rather than final authority.

question_text: According to the lecture, when is more predictive power in credit scoring useful?
hint: Predictive power is not enough on its own. The lecture names three things the institution must be able to do with the result.
correct_answer_citation: Week 03 — Credit Scoring Beyond Static Rules

options.option_text: Always, because better rank ordering of risk outweighs every other concern.
options.option_explanation: The lecture qualifies this: more predictive power is useful only if the institution can explain, govern, and operationalize the result.

options.option_text: Only when the model keeps to the same patterns that traditional scorecards use.
options.option_explanation: Modern scoring systems are valued because they can incorporate richer behavioral, transactional, and application-level patterns than traditional scorecards alone.

options.option_text: Only when it removes the review option and leaves just approve or decline.
options.option_explanation: The lecture describes better segmentation of approve, review, and decline decisions, so review remains one of the three.

options.option_text: Only if the institution can explain, govern, and operationalize the result.
options.option_explanation: Correct. More predictive power is useful only if the institution can explain, govern, and operationalize the result.

question_text: Who does the lecture say lending model explanations need to be meaningful to?
hint: The lecture names three audiences, and one group that is not enough on its own.
correct_answer_citation: Week 03 — Explainability, Fairness, and Adverse Action

options.option_text: Data scientists, because they are the people who build and tune the model.
options.option_explanation: Institutions need explanations that are meaningful to risk managers, regulators, and customers, not only to data scientists.

options.option_text: Risk managers, regulators, and customers, not only data scientists.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Institutions need explanations that are meaningful to risk managers, regulators, and customers, not only to data scientists.

options.option_text: Regulators alone, because they are the ones who examine lending models.
options.option_explanation: Regulators are one audience, but the lecture also names risk managers and customers.

options.option_text: Only the teams that handle the cases a model sends to manual review.
options.option_explanation: Being sent to manual review is one of the outcomes that puts lending models under scrutiny. It does not define who explanations are for.

question_text: Why do static fraud rules degrade quickly, according to the lecture?
hint: Fraud is described as adaptive. Think about what attackers learn.
correct_answer_citation: Week 03 — Fraud Detection as an Adversarial Problem

options.option_text: Case feedback and device signals overwrite the rules as time goes on.
options.option_explanation: The lecture presents device signals and case feedback as inputs that effective systems combine with historical patterns, not as something that breaks rules.

options.option_text: Historical patterns stop being recorded once the rules are in place.
options.option_explanation: Effective systems still combine historical patterns with other signals; the lecture does not say they stop being recorded.

options.option_text: Adversaries learn the thresholds and change their timing or channel.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Fraud is adaptive, so static rules degrade quickly when adversaries learn the thresholds and change timing, identity, channel, or transaction structure.

options.option_text: Rules become too expensive to run as transaction volumes keep growing.
options.option_explanation: Cost is not the reason given. Static rules remain useful, but they degrade quickly when adversaries learn the thresholds.

question_text: How does the lecture say portfolio recommendations should be treated?
hint: Consider what would have to explicitly permit a different treatment.
correct_answer_citation: Week 03 — Portfolio Construction and Decision Support

options.option_text: As automated trades by default, since the tools can rebalance exposures faster.
options.option_explanation: The default is the reverse: recommendations are decision support unless governance explicitly permits automated execution.

options.option_text: As decision support unless governance explicitly permits automated execution.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Portfolio recommendations should be treated as decision support unless governance explicitly permits automated execution.

options.option_text: As reliable in any market, since the tools already test scenarios under constraints.
options.option_explanation: Their usefulness depends on assumptions about liquidity, turnover, transaction costs, and risk appetite, so they are not reliable regardless of conditions.

options.option_text: As independent of any assumptions about liquidity, turnover, or transaction costs.
options.option_explanation: The lecture says their usefulness depends on assumptions about liquidity, turnover, transaction costs, and risk appetite.

question_text: When is a model inventory useful, according to the lecture?
hint: A list of models is not enough by itself. Ask what it has to be connected to.
correct_answer_citation: Week 03 — Model Governance Across the Lifecycle

options.option_text: When it is tied to actual decision rights and review cadence.
options.option_explanation: Correct. A model inventory is useful only if it is tied to actual decision rights and review cadence.

options.option_text: When it lists every model, whether or not anyone ever reviews them.
options.option_explanation: A list alone is not enough; the lecture says an inventory is useful only if it is tied to actual decision rights and review cadence.

options.option_text: When it covers development and leaves deployment to individual teams.
options.option_explanation: Institutions need controls across data sourcing, development, validation, deployment, monitoring, and retirement.

options.option_text: When it removes the need to document how exceptions are handled.
options.option_explanation: Governance must clarify how exceptions are documented; an inventory does not remove that need.

question_text: When does the lecture say generative systems are weakest in finance?
hint: The lecture contrasts support roles with a role where nobody checks the output.
correct_answer_citation: Week 03 — Generative AI in Finance: High-Value Uses and Red Lines

options.option_text: When used for summarization and knowledge retrieval across the firm.
options.option_explanation: Summarization and knowledge retrieval are where the lecture says generative systems are strongest.

options.option_text: When used to support analysts with drafting and coding assistance.
options.option_explanation: Drafting, coding assistance, and analyst support are listed among their strongest uses.

options.option_text: When red lines for autonomous use are set before experimentation spreads.
options.option_explanation: Defining explicit red lines before experimentation spreads across teams is what the lecture recommends, not a weakness.

options.option_text: When used as unchecked authorities for regulated advice or disclosures.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Generative systems are weakest when used as unchecked authorities for regulated advice, formal disclosures, or final risk approval.
